title: Life is a campaign
hookLine: to live is to be a soldier; complaints don't help (Letters 96)

lines: THE CAR, THE TOOTH, THE EMAIL.
cards: Are you still complaining? That, more or less, is how Seneca opens the ninety-sixth letter. From his reply, we can guess Lucilius's mood: things keep going wrong, and it isn't fair.
Some weeks go like that. The car, then the tooth, then the email. Seneca's answer is short, almost impatient: a single picture of what a human life is, taken from the army on the march.

teach.b: First, the tax. All the things that make us groan and shudder, Seneca says, are the tax of being alive: illness, loss, delays, worry. Nobody is excused from the tax, and grumbling doesn't lower it.
Second, agreeing, not just obeying. Then he says something personal.

teach.h: I DON'T OBEY GOD; I AGREE.
teach.b: In these things, I don't obey God; I agree with him. I follow willingly, not because I must.

For a Stoic, God here is the reason that orders the universe, and agreeing means meeting what comes as part of a whole you trust, instead of being dragged. Third, the line. In Latin: vivere, Lucili, militare est.

teach.h: TO LIVE IS TO BE A SOLDIER.
teach.b: To live, Lucilius, is to be a soldier.
Those who scramble up the rocks and down the ravines, who take the hard marches and the dangerous missions, aren't the unlucky ones. They're the ones the commander trusts. Fourth, why it helps.
A soldier on campaign doesn't take mud personally. The march is hard because it's a march. We met a cousin of this on day four hundred twenty-seven, with Epictetus at his post.

Seneca's version is about attitude on the road: stop asking why this is happening to me, and start asking how to carry it well. In a few weeks, we'll hear an emperor who actually was on campaign say something similar.

how: Stoic practitioners often treat ordinary hardships as part of the terms of life, trading the question 'why me?' for 'how do I carry this well?'

o: to live is to be a soldier on a hard march
a soldier's oath to obey every order given
a call to fight anyone who does you wrong

p: to live is to be a soldier

s: Seneca says hard things only happen to unlucky people
they're the tax of being alive; nobody is excused.
Seneca says he agrees with God rather than merely obeying
he follows willingly, not because he must.
Seneca says complaining lowers the cost of hardship

games.q: you've had a week of one setback after another and you're writing to a friend to complain. what does Seneca write back?
o: you're right, life has singled you out.
to live is to be a soldier: this is the march.
games.why: Seneca says hardships are the tax of living, and the hard missions go to those the commander trusts.

practice: Name one hard thing you're carrying this week, a delay, a pain, a task you dread, and picture it as one ravine on a long march.
Notice the complaint that wants to ride along with it, why me, it's not fair, and set that down beside the road. Without the complaint, feel how heavy the thing itself really is.

wordCard.voice: Militare est. Seneca's line: to live is to be a soldier; hardship is the tax of life, and complaint doesn't lower it. Today's word.
